summary: Identity service ships register/login/refresh as functional handlers; the remaining 8 endpoints (logout, profile.read/update, all 5 address endpoints) are explicit 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED_MVP stubs documented in the README. SQL is fully parameterized via pgx; ES256 keys are env-sourced via notEmpty PEM (no hardcoding); the refresh-rotation single-tx (UPDATE-then-INSERT with RowsAffected==1 check) is implemented correctly in storage_refresh_token.go RotateInTx; only jti is persisted (not the JWT body). The two material defects are (1) password hashing uses HashSha256EncodePepper — i.e. base64(sha256(plaintext+pepper)) with NO per-user salt and NO work factor (CWE-916/CWE-759, ASVS V2.4.1) — which the dev README ID-DEC-4 acknowledges and defers, and (2) login does a Go == compare on the hash instead of subtle.ConstantTimeCompare (CWE-208, ASVS V2.4.7). Both are HIGH code_security_issue. The spec itself induced the password-hash gap by telling dev to call common/hash.Hash with bcrypt cost 12 — an API that does not exist in common/hash (only SHA-256 variants are exported); that is the one spec_induced_security_issue HIGH and routes to Tech-Designer to either extend common/hash or adopt golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt directly. Medium findings cover token-type confusion (no tokenType==refresh check on /auth/refresh), shared signing key for access+refresh (defense-in-depth gap permitted but not required by contracts.json), missing request-size cap, missing email normalization (case-sensitive UNIQUE on TEXT email creates account confusion + login miss), unvalidated phone field on register (TD pattern not enforced — handler_register.go has no binding tag on Phone), no rate-limit on auth routes (CWE-307), and the absence of logout meaning a stolen 30-day refresh token has no user-driven kill-switch. Low advisories cover hash-algo migration trap (no algo discriminator stored alongside password_hash), brittle deferred-rollback pattern in RotateInTx, zero clock-skew tolerance in ValidateClaims, and envelope-code shape (wrapper uses '0000' literal vs the contract's documented 'SUCCESS' enum value — shared library deviation, out of identity scope but flagged).

findings.description: Password hashing uses common/hash.HashSha256EncodePepper, which computes base64(sha256(plaintext+pepper)) with NO per-user salt and NO work factor. SHA-256 is a general-purpose hash, not a password KDF — modern GPUs crack billions of SHA-256 hashes/sec, so a database leak makes every password trivially recoverable. The shared 16-char pepper offers only superficial protection (single offline pepper guess applies to all users; if pepper leaks via env or core dump, all hashes fall). Service.Register stores this in users.password_hash; Login compares against it. The TD ID-DEC-4 specified bcrypt cost 12 + pepper via common/hash, but common/hash does not export a bcrypt function — only SHA-256 variants. Dev shipped the SHA-256 variant and documented the gap in README ID-DEC-4 as deferred to v2 instead of escalating. CWE-916 (use of password hash with insufficient computational effort), CWE-759 (use of one-way hash without a salt), OWASP ASVS V2.4.1, OWASP API2:2023.
findings.recommendation: Extend common/hash with HashBcrypt(plain) []byte and CompareBcrypt(hash, plain) bool that wrap golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt at cost 12 (or use argon2id via golang.org/x/crypto/argon2 with params m=64MB, t=3, p=2). Replace HashSha256EncodePepper calls in identity service.Register and service.Login. Use bcrypt's built-in salt; the existing pepper can be kept as HMAC-pre-step (HMAC-SHA256(pepper, password) → bcrypt) to defend against DB-only leaks. Add a password_hash_algo column (or version prefix '$bcrypt12$' inside password_hash) to enable lazy rehash on next login when v2 ships. Replace the '!=' compare in Login with bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword which is constant-time internally — this also closes REV-IDENT-002. Existing SHA-256 hashes need a one-time migration: on next successful login under SHA-256, rehash with bcrypt and update the row in the same transaction.

findings.description: Login compares the computed hash to the stored hash with Go's `!=` string operator: `if computed != user.PasswordHash`. Go string comparison short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking timing information about how many leading bytes match. While the AUTH-007 'always run hash even if user not found' mitigation correctly prevents the user-enumeration timing oracle, it does not protect the hash-comparison step itself. Combined with the deterministic SHA-256 hash (REV-IDENT-001), an attacker who can submit many login attempts and measure response time can in principle perform a timing-based byte-by-byte recovery of the stored hash, then crack the hash offline. CWE-208 (observable timing discrepancy), OWASP ASVS V2.4.7.
findings.recommendation: Replace `if computed != user.PasswordHash` with `if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(computed), []byte(user.PasswordHash)) != 1`. Import crypto/subtle. Note: once REV-IDENT-001 is fixed by adopting bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword, this finding is automatically closed because bcrypt's compare is constant-time internally — but until then, the subtle.ConstantTimeCompare patch is a one-line stop-gap that should land immediately. Validation: add a unit test with two stored hashes differing only in the last byte and assert the timing distribution is statistically indistinguishable from two hashes differing in the first byte (or simpler: assert subtle.ConstantTimeCompare is the call used).

findings.description: TD instructs the developer to 'use common/hash.Hash(password) for bcrypt cost 12 with pepper' — but common/hash exposes only HashSha256Encode, HashSha256EncodeSalt, and HashSha256EncodePepper (see common/hash/hash_manager.go). There is no bcrypt API in common/hash and no `Hash` method at all. Faced with this gap, dev (correctly) wrote ID-DEC-4 in the service README acknowledging the downgrade to SHA-256+pepper as MVP and deferring bcrypt to v2. The TD itself is the root cause: it referenced a non-existent API and provided no guidance on what to do when the lib gap appears. This is the single spec_induced_security_issue HIGH. CWE-1390 (weak authentication mechanism) at the design layer.
findings.recommendation: Tech-Designer revises ID-DEC-4 to one of: (a) MUST extend common/hash to add HashBcrypt + CompareBcrypt at cost 12 (golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt; last CVE check 2025-08, no open advisories) before identity registers any user, or (b) MUST use golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt directly inside identity service.Register/Login. Add a TD field `common_lib_gap_handling: 'block — escalate to Tech-Designer for API extension; do not silently substitute weaker primitive'` so future devs do not re-make this judgement call. Update implementation_hints to reference the actual API name once the lib is extended. Add an explicit acceptance test 'register_password_is_bcrypt_hashed' that decodes the stored password_hash and asserts it begins with '$2a$12$' or '$argon2id$'.

findings.description: Refresh handler verifies signature, parses claims, and validates iss/aud/exp — but never asserts `claims.Extra['tokenType'] == 'refresh'`. Both signers in router/deps.go use the SAME private key (cfg.JWT.PrivateKeyPEM) — only TTL differs — so an access JWT and a refresh JWT are cryptographically interchangeable and pass identical signature/iss/aud checks. Today the only protection against access-token-as-refresh-token confusion is the refresh_tokens DB lookup (an access JTI is not in the table → AUTH_REVOKED). That is fragile defense-in-depth: if a future endpoint ever accepts the refresh JWT for any reason without a DB lookup, type confusion becomes exploitable. The signAccess and signRefresh functions DO emit `tokenType: access|refresh` in Extra claims — the Refresh handler simply does not read it. CWE-345 (insufficient verification of data authenticity), OWASP API8:2023, ASVS V3.5.2.
findings.recommendation: In service.Refresh, after ValidateClaims succeeds, add: `if tt, _ := claims.Extra['tokenType'].(string); tt != 'refresh' { return ..., ErrAuthInvalid }`. Add the inverse check in any future middleware that consumes access tokens (`tt != 'access' → reject`). Defense in depth: in router/deps.go, source a second env var JWT_REFRESH_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM (and matching public key) so access and refresh use different keypairs — contracts.json line 43 explicitly allows this ('separate keypair allowed'). Backward-compat: default JWT_REFRESH_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM to JWT_PRIVATE_KEY_PEM if unset, with a deprecation warning at startup.

findings.description: Email is passed straight from JSON into INSERT and SELECT without normalization. The users.email column is `TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL` (migrations/001_users.up.sql:9) — a case-sensitive comparison. Two consequences: (a) `Alice@example.com` and `alice@example.com` register as two distinct accounts, creating account confusion and complicating support / data-subject requests under PDPA/GDPR; (b) a user who registers as `Alice@x.com` and later logs in with `alice@x.com` (browser autocomplete lowercases) will hit AUTH_INVALID — usability bug that tempts users to weaker passwords or password reuse. CWE-178 (case-sensitivity inconsistency), ASVS V2.1.4.
findings.recommendation: In Register and Login, normalize email at the service boundary: `email = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(email))` before any DB call. Optionally migrate the schema to CITEXT, or replace UNIQUE(email) with a functional unique index `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_lower_idx ON users (lower(email))` and update GetByEmail to `WHERE lower(email) = lower($1)`. The Go-side normalization closes the gap immediately without a migration and is the smaller diff for MVP. Preserve raw-cased email in a separate `email_display` column if marketing wants to send 'Hi Alice@example.com' formatted mail.

findings.description: The Phone field on registerRequest has NO Gin binding tag: `Phone *string `json:"phone"`'`. TD validation_rules require phone to match `^[0-9+\- ]{7,20}$` when present. As shipped, an attacker can submit `phone: '<script>alert(1)</script>' + ('A'*10000)` and it lands in users.phone unfiltered. Postgres TEXT will accept it; downstream consumers (admin UI, order shipping label, SMS gateway) face stored-XSS / injection / DoS exposure. CWE-20 (improper input validation), ASVS V5.1.4.
findings.recommendation: Change to: `Phone *string `json:"phone" binding:"omitempty,min=7,max=20,phone_pattern"``. Register a custom validator `phone_pattern` against Gin's validator.v10 instance that compiles `^[0-9+\- ]{7,20}$` once. Apply the same pattern on profile.update and address.create when those are un-stubbed. Add a unit test register_with_malicious_phone_returns_400.

findings.description: No request-body size cap on register/login/refresh. main.go sets http.Server.MaxHeaderBytes=1<<20 but the JSON body is read by c.ShouldBindJSON via Gin's default unbounded reader. An attacker can POST a 50MB refreshToken field, causing pgx to copy a giant string and the server to spend memory/CPU on JSON decode. Easy DoS. CWE-770 (allocation of resources without limits).
findings.recommendation: Add Gin middleware to the auth group that wraps c.Request.Body in `http.MaxBytesReader(c.Writer, c.Request.Body, 16<<10)` (16 KiB is generous for JWT+JSON envelope; tune per endpoint). Or add it as a global middleware after Recovery. Tests: TestRegisterWithOversizeBodyReturns413.

findings.description: No rate-limit middleware on /auth/register, /auth/login, /auth/refresh. The router applies SecurityHeaders, AccessLog, Timeout — and that is the entire chain. /auth/login is open to credential-stuffing at line speed. /auth/register's deliberate 409 EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED on duplicate (per TD error_contract) is a designed enumeration oracle that is acceptable WHEN paired with rate-limiting; without rate-limiting, an attacker enumerates the user base in minutes. CWE-307 (improper restriction of excessive auth attempts), OWASP API4:2023.
findings.recommendation: Add common/middleware.RateLimit (or ulule/limiter) keyed by client IP at e.g. 10/min for /auth/login and 5/min for /auth/register, 30/min for /auth/refresh. If common/middleware does not yet expose a rate-limit primitive, this is a second common-lib gap to surface to Tech-Designer for the platform team. In production the upstream gateway (Kong/APISIX/CloudFront) is the more robust place; document it as a NOT-IN-SERVICE-LAYER decision if that is the chosen direction, and add a smoke test that rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit-*) are present in responses.

findings.description: Logout returns 501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED_MVP. Refresh-token TTL is 30 days. Until logout ships, a refresh token captured by an attacker (XSS, malicious extension, MITM on a misconfigured client) is valid for the full 30-day window with no user-driven revocation path. The only kill-switch is admin-side `UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at=NOW() WHERE jti=X`. BA acceptance test `logout_revokes_refresh_token` (AC-08) cannot pass. CWE-613 (insufficient session expiration) — partial.
findings.recommendation: Ship logout in this PR — the storage layer already has `Revoke(ctx, jti)` (storage_refresh_token.go:85-89). Handler needs to: (1) extract user_id from middleware-injected claims, (2) parse refreshToken from body, (3) verify jti.user_id == authenticated user_id (anti cross-user logout per TD logout.implementation_hints line 4), (4) call rts.Revoke. About 30 LOC. If logout truly cannot ship in this PR, document a compensating control: shorten refresh TTL to 24h, OR provide an admin endpoint that BA acceptance can drive, OR mark AC-08 as deferred with sign-off.

findings.description: Deferred rollback closure captures local `err`. On the happy path the function returns after `tx.Commit(ctx)` succeeds; the deferred closure then sees err==nil and skips rollback (correct). On the rows==0 branch the explicit `tx.Rollback(ctx)` already fires before return, so the deferred check sees rows==0 and an err that may be nil — also correct. Net behavior is right today, but the pattern is brittle: any future edit that adds a `return 0, fmt.Errorf(...)` without setting the local err first would skip rollback. Use the idiomatic `defer tx.Rollback(ctx)` (Postgres treats rollback-after-commit as a no-op).
findings.recommendation: Replace lines 42-46 with `defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback(ctx) }()` — unconditional. Remove the explicit `_ = tx.Rollback(ctx)` inside the rows==0 branch since the deferred call covers it. This is purely a robustness improvement; current behavior is correct.

findings.description: users.password_hash stores a bare base64-SHA256 string with no algorithm or version prefix. When REV-IDENT-001 is fixed by introducing bcrypt, migrating the DB requires either (a) forcing every user to reset password (UX disaster for an MVP user base if it grows), or (b) a lazy-rehash flow that needs to know which algorithm produced each row. Without an algo column or a structural prefix in the hash itself, the lazy-rehash flow cannot distinguish SHA-256 hashes from bcrypt hashes and will need to brute-detect — fragile. CWE-1390 partial.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) add migration 004_password_hash_algo.up.sql: `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN password_hash_algo TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'sha256_pepper_v1';` and set it to 'bcrypt12_pepper_v1' on rehash; or (b) prefix the hash itself: store `'$shappilot_sha256_pepper_v1$' + base64hash` and bcrypt rows naturally start with `$2a$`. Option (b) is one-column and self-describing.

findings.description: ValidateClaims uses `payload.Iat > now` with zero clock-skew tolerance. Cross-pod or NTP drift of even a second can produce sporadic 'token not yet valid' errors at issue time, especially under load when issue-then-immediate-use is common. ASVS V3.2.3 recommends a small (e.g. 30s) skew tolerance. Same for `payload.Exp < now` on the trailing edge. Out of identity scope (lives in common/token), but identity is the only service that calls it for authentication-critical paths today.
findings.recommendation: Common-lib change: add `const ClockSkewTolerance = 30 * time.Second` and adjust to `if payload.Exp + int64(ClockSkewTolerance.Seconds()) < now` and `if payload.Iat - int64(ClockSkewTolerance.Seconds()) > now`. Surface to common-lib owner; identity does not own this file.

findings.description: All success responses emit `code: '0000'` (wrapper.CodeSuccess literal) instead of the contract-documented `code: 'SUCCESS'` (contracts.json line 117 cross-cutting.error-codes registry). Same on every error code: handler_login.go line 39 emits `code: 'AUTH_INVALID'` correctly, but success path emits the numeric '0000'. Either the contract is wrong (registry should list '0000') or every service is shipping non-conformant success envelopes. This is a shared-library deviation that affects every service, not just identity — out of identity-component scope but worth flagging.
findings.recommendation: Tech-Designer / common-lib owner reconciles the cross-cutting.error-codes registry against common/wrapper/codes.go. If the contract is canonical, change CodeSuccess to 'SUCCESS' (and CodeBadRequest to 'VALIDATION_ERROR', etc.). If the implementation is canonical, update contracts.json. Either way, identity does not need to change in isolation.
